titulo: What goes to the queue (and what stays with you)
lead: Not every task should go to the queue. Before you install anything, you run your list through three questions and come away with a table: runs on its own, runs with a gate, or stays with you.
objetivo: sort ten of your tasks into runs on its own, with a gate, or stays with you, and say where each gate goes.
hero_alt: Hands sorting paper cards into three piles on a table.

aprende.t: What should not go to the queue
Your queue on paper, with ten rows

nos.detalhe: Start with what you repeat. A task that shows up every week, with the same kind of input, is a natural candidate.

itens.sub: a link, a file, a topic
a file or text that you read

nos.detalhe: Clear input and a result you can check: it goes into the queue. If the result also goes out into the world (it publishes, sends, spends credit), it gets a gate before that step.
Internal use and a cheap mistake: if it comes out bad, you just redo it. It runs all night without asking for anything.
The agent does the heavy part and stops. You read, fix, and approve. Only then does it go on to publish or spend.

itens.t: Vague input or a delicate decision

nos.detalhe: A request that needs a conversation ("improve this"), a business decision, or an irreversible action with no way to review it. It goes back to the queue when you can describe the input and the result.

secoes.legenda: Tap each block. The question that changes the outcome the most is the third one: a consequence outside calls for a gate.

secoes.titulo: The three questions, one by one
secoes.sub: With examples of what runs today in inemaccbot.

texto: The queue doesn't chat with you in the middle. The task has to fit on one line: a link, a file path, or a topic.
The inemaccbot skills show the format: transcrever: https://…, explicativo: <assunto> | vertical, imagem: uma raposa ruiva na neve | ratio=16:9.

exemplo.texto: "Give the presentation a polish." Improve what, and how far? It stays with you, or it becomes a concrete input.

texto: In the morning you'll look at the result. If it's a file (text, video, image), you check it in minutes. If it's "I did a bunch of things", there's no way to know whether it came out right.
In the bot, this is a contract: the agent ends with RESULT: <caminho>, and the bot checks that the file exists and has the expected extension.
Publishing on behalf of the company, sending to a customer, spending paid credit: this is where the gate comes in. The agent prepares and stops; you approve.
Transcribing a meeting for you to read yourself has no consequences outside. It runs on its own.

exemplo.texto: /promoavatar writes the texts for each audience and stops. Only after your approval does it move on to the video and the reel.

passos.titulo: Is redoing it from scratch acceptable?
texto: This question doesn't change whether it goes into the queue; it changes the type. If redoing from scratch is cheap, a single skill (one step) is enough. If there's partial work that would be absurd to throw away, the right choice is a flow (several phases, with state and resume).
You'll use both in lessons 5 and 6.

blocos.rot: Request for your agent to review the table
blocos.conteudo:
Read the file fila-no-papel.md. For each line, check:
1. Does the input fit on one line (link, file, or subject)?
2. Is the result a file or text that can be checked?
3. Is there an outside consequence (publishing, sending, spending)? If so, is there a gate marked?
Point out the lines that should change destination and say why. Do not change the file.

abas.html:
• Row 4 ("organize the calendar"): vague input. I suggest "stays with you" or rewriting it as "list this week's calendar conflicts".
  • Row 7 ("reply to customer emails"): outside consequence with no gate. I suggest "queue with gate": the agent drafts, you send.
  • The rest are consistent.

• No gate in ten rows: check that nothing is published or sent.
  • Every row has a gate: you'll spend the morning approving; see what is internal use only.
  • Result "several files" or "improve": hard to check.

secoes.sub: Prerequisite: steps 1 and 2 of the program.

exercicios.texto: Fill in the table with ten repetitive tasks from your work. For each one: input in one line, checkable result, destination, and where the gate goes. Ask your agent to review it using the template above.
exercicios.pronto: all 10 rows are filled in and at least two have a gate.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: In which task is the human gate most important?
opcoes: Summarizing PDFs for you to read yourself.
Publishing a post on behalf of the company.
Listing the files in a folder.
perguntas.explica: The gate goes before anything with an outside consequence: publishing, sending, spending. Internal use where a mistake is cheap can run on its own.

perguntas.p: Should "give the presentation a polish" go in the queue?
opcoes: Yes, as long as it uses the most expensive model.
Not yet: the input is vague. Either it stays with you, or it becomes a concrete request.
perguntas.explica: The queue doesn't talk to you in the middle of the night. Without a clear input, there's no way to check that the result came out right.

perguntas.p: A task has several stages and the middle one is expensive. If the last stage fails, you don't want to redo everything. Which type should you use?
opcoes: One flow, which saves the state of each phase and resumes from the one that failed.
None: expensive tasks don't go in the queue.
perguntas.explica: A skill makes sense when redoing from scratch is acceptable. When partial work is valuable, the flow saves each phase and /refazer resumes from the one that failed.
